title: Where did Ruhee go wrong with fifty six and sixty three?
description: Two children write the same two numbers as products. One finds no shared factor and the other finds seven in both. The board lists the factors of fifty six and shows how many of them one product reveals, then Keeko doubts that one pair of factors is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: one product such as fourteen times four names only two factors, so a missing match proves nothing. Watch for students who think one pair of factors shows every factor of the number.

source: Teacher asks: Are 56 and 63 co-prime? Ruhee writes 56 = 14 ×
video_script.why: The child sees that one product shows only two factors of a number, so a common factor can stay hidden.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, fifty six and sixty three, written two ways
video_script.anchor: the numbers fifty six and sixty three written as products by the two children of the book
video_script.wrong_answer: one pair of factors shows every factor of the number
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes fourteen and four, the pair from one product, to be all the factors of fifty six.
video_script.payoff_line: Ruhee looked at only some factors and missed the common factor seven

final_answer.value: 56 = 14 × 4 shows only 14 and 4 as factors of 56, not all; the common factor 7 was missed
final_answer.spoken: Ruhee looked at only some factors and missed the common factor seven

names.Leeza: the child who finds that seven is a common factor of fifty six and sixty three
names.Ruhee: the child who writes fifty six as fourteen times four and wrongly says the numbers are co-prime

maths_rules: 56 = 7 × 8 and 63 = 9 × 7, so 7 is a factor of both numbers
factors of 56: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 28, 56 (eight factors); 14 × 4 shows two of them
7 is a common factor, so 56 and 63 are not co-prime
video_script.design: The two products of each child sit side by side. The full list of factors of fifty six shows how little one product reveals.

<bookmark mark='teacher'/>The teacher asks if they are co-prime.
<bookmark mark='anshu'/>Ruhee writes fifty six as fourteen times four, and sixty three as twenty one times three.
<bookmark mark='guna'/>Leeza writes fifty six as seven times eight, and sixty three as nine times seven.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Leeza is right, but where did Ruhee go wrong?

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one pair of factors shows every factor of the number, so Ruhee did nothing wrong.
<bookmark mark='look'/>Look at fifty six again. It has eight factors, but fourteen times four shows only two.
<bookmark mark='hide'/>The other six factors stay hidden, and one of them can be shared.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>One pair cannot show all the others, and a shared factor can hide.
